title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

items.title: [WIRED] Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed. Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant.

items.title: [Fast Company] South Korea’s bank hacks offer a warning about AI-powered cyberattacks
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Some of South Korea’s biggest banks have been hacked with the assistance of an artificial intelligence agent, opening up a new front in the AI and cybersecurity worlds.

Officials say at least seven financial firms were included in the attack, which saw personal information for 68,000 people stolen, including annual income and loan limits. This marks one of the first times AI tools have been used to disrupt global financial stalwarts.

It’s notable, since banks and other financial institutions typically have a higher level of security than other businesses or even some government agencies. Officials say they haven’t identified the people responsible for the attacks, which originated from over two dozen IP addresses spread out over several countries, including the U.S. and Japan. (Hackers frequently spoof their IP address to remain anonymous.)

South Korean officials are urging banks to boost their defenses. And the intrusions could serve as a warning shot for banks in the United States and other countries as well.

“AI gives attackers more opportunities to exploit gaps before defenders respond,” Yagub Rahimov, CEO of Polygraf AI, tells Fast Company. “My advice to bank leadership is to take a step back and invest in threat mapping. Trace the actual paths to sensitive data through employee activities, vendor connections, applications, APIs [application programming interfaces], and human and machine identities. They need to identify the systems that are reachable.”

The hackers apparently used Artex AI, an open-source agent developed in China, which ironically was designed as a cybersecurity tool that helped users find vulnerabilities in their networks. Artex has since updated its user guidelines to say the tool should not be used for malicious reasons.

AI-assisted hacking on the rise

While the attacks on the South Korean banks represent a new level, there has been a consistent uptick in AI-assisted hacking for some time now. A July report from the SANS Institute found that 78% of organizations saw either a confirmed or suspected AI-enabled attack in the past year.

The method of those attacks was evenly spread, though. Occurrences of phishing, deepfakes, and vulnerability exploitation were all virtually the same.

“AI tools are maturing, and so are the criminals using them—they moved from scaling phishing campaigns to autonomously probing defenses, chaining exploits, and adapting mid-attack,” Vakaris Noreika, cybersecurity expert at NordLayer Intelligence by NordStellar, tells Fast Company. “Going forward, we should expect attacks to grow in both scale and sophistication, which means defenses must keep pace with an AI-enabled threat landscape.”

The SANS Institute study showed a disparity between concern over possible AI-enhanced hacks and actual preparedness. Virtually every respondent—some 95%—said they believe threat actors are using AI today to enhance their attacks, with 58% saying they believe the use of AI is significant. Yet only 16% say they have shifted their priority to defend against such attacks.

Corrupting a tool

While Artex was designed to help protect users, the hackers’ use of this agent shows the range of possible threats that exist.

“The same capability that helps a security team investigate a weakness is also being used by an attacker to identify gaps for malicious purposes,” Rahimov says. “AI can connect tasks that previously required more manual work, making repeated attacks more economical—but even this can be turned around. Businesses should prepare for that capability to spread across tools and operators.”

Noreika warns that it’s not just smaller AI agent tools that can be corrupted, either. Most open-source AI models from a major lab possess the same advanced capabilities to hide malicious activity as security testing. That should put CEOs of banks and any other business on alert.

“The best way for companies to protect themselves is to adopt a hacker’s mindset—leveraging the very same AI tools to evaluate, stress-test, and strengthen their own security defenses,” Noreika says.

Regular http service remains unaffected.
